extracted.intended_audience: readers of Mark Twain correspondence and biography; literary scholars and general readers interested in writing and literary judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and writing guidance embedded in Mark Twain's letters and associated commentary (about magazine-writing, autobiography, literary quality, and working conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-elaboration and thin motives (critique of Sir Walter Scott)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Interest? Why, it is impossible to feel an interest in these bloodless shams, these milk-and-water humbugs. And oh, the poverty of the invention!...Sir Walter usually gives himself away when he arranges for a situation--elaborates, and elaborates, and elaborates, till if you live to get to it you don't believe in it when it happens.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manufacture situations by excessive elaboration or provide inadequate reasons for events; over-explaining or piling on contrivances makes readers disbelieve and lose interest. Aim for believable motives and economy in arranging plot situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: What makes a great writer (bring something new)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Each brought to his time some new blood, new ideas,--turned a new current into the stream...It seems to be the unconventionally honest man...who has to express himself in his own big way because the conventional way isn't big enough.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness comes from introducing genuinely new currents or perspectives into literature—an honestly unconventional voice that offers fresh ideas rather than merely polished conventionality. Value originality that resonates with deep human concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books that claim unreserved interest (combination of humor and depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merwin's praise: Twain's books are those "to which I could surrender myself without reservation...they've brought something really new into our literature...Shakespeare plunged deep into the deep, sad things of life; and so, in a different way...has Mark Twain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that endures often balances buoyant, dramatic depiction of life with emotional depth—able to make readers laugh and also move them to tears. Avoid pigeonholing such work as mere 'humor' when it accesses profound themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiography: truth between the lines
rubrics_metrics.description: “An autobiography is the truest of all books; for while it inevitably consists mainly of extinctions of the truth, shirkings of the truth, partial revealments of the truth, with hardly an instance of plain straight truth, the remorseless truth is there, between the lines..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that autobiographical truth is often indirect: authors will omit or soften facts, but genuine truth emerges between the lines. Use safeguards (editorial discipline, 'court of last resort') but trust that unvarnished reality can still be conveyed by tone, implication, and candid detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine-writing practice: expect heavy revision and editorial filters
rubrics_metrics.description: “Magazining is difficult work because every third page represents 2 pages that you have put in the fire; (because you are nearly sure to start wrong twice) and so when you have finished an article and are willing to let it go to print it represents only 10 cents a word instead of 30."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazine pieces typically require discarding substantial material and multiple restarts. Anticipate high revision costs and lower per-word returns; rely on trusted readers/editors (Twain's 'court of last resort' Livy) to approve and help identify pieces that 'start right.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive working conditions (environmental factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This secluded and silent solitude this clean, soft air and this enchanting view of Florence...are the right conditions for work. They are a persistent inspiration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster solitude, quiet, healthy air, and inspiring surroundings to promote focused creative work. Physical environment can materially affect productivity and the ability to sustain writing routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer spontaneous honors to solicited ones (attitude toward recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Spontaneous and unpremeditated honors...are beyond all price and are a treasure for life...I am humanly fond of honors that happen but chary of those that come by canvass and intention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering public recognition or honors, value those that arise unsolicited as more meaningful; be cautious about participating in arrangements that make one a party to one's own exalting, since solicited honors may feel less authentic.
